subject: Environment
topic: Ecology and biogeochemical cycles — mixed tiers
description: Water, carbon, nitrogen cycles; ecosystem structure

questions.stem: In the nitrogen cycle, nitrogen-fixing bacteria that live in the root nodules of leguminous plants belong to the genus:

options.option_text: Pseudomonas
Rhizobium
Lactobacillus
Escherichia

questions.explanation: Rhizobium — symbiotic nitrogen-fixing bacteria in the root nodules of legumes (pulses, chickpea, soybean, groundnut). They convert atmospheric N₂ into ammonium that the plant can use. Free-living soil nitrogen fixers — Azotobacter, Clostridium. Cyanobacteria (Nostoc, Anabaena) fix nitrogen in water-logged paddy fields. Lactobacillus — curdles milk. Pseudomonas, E. coli — common bacteria but not primary N-fixers in this context.

questions.stem: The carbon cycle's main natural 'carbon sink' — which absorbs roughly a quarter of annual human CO₂ emissions — is the:

options.option_text: Atmosphere
Ocean
Ice sheets
Volcanic rocks

questions.explanation: Oceans take up about 25-30 % of human CO₂ emissions each year (forming carbonic acid — source of ocean acidification, pH down from 8.2 to ~8.1 since industrial times). Land plants and soils take up another ~25 %. The remaining ~50 % stays in the atmosphere and drives warming. Phytoplankton and coral polyps are key in the 'biological pump' that moves carbon into deep ocean sediments.

questions.stem: The process by which water evaporates from plant leaves into the atmosphere is called:

options.option_text: Respiration
Transpiration
Condensation
Precipitation

questions.explanation: Transpiration — water vapour leaves the plant mostly through tiny pores on the leaf surface called stomata. Helps cool the plant and pulls up the nutrient-bearing water column from roots. Globally, plants return about 40 % of terrestrial rainfall to the atmosphere via transpiration. Respiration — cellular energy production releasing CO₂. Condensation and precipitation — parts of the physical water cycle, not plant processes.

questions.stem: The number of different species living in a given area is called its:

options.option_text: Biomass
Species richness
Population density
Niche width

questions.explanation: Species richness — the count of different species in an ecosystem (α-diversity in Whittaker's scheme). β-diversity — turnover between communities. γ-diversity — overall diversity in a region. Biomass is the total mass of living material. Population density — individuals of one species per unit area. A 'niche' describes the role a species plays and the conditions it needs.

questions.stem: Of the following biomes, the one with the highest biological productivity (biomass produced per unit time per unit area) is:

options.option_text: Tundra
Tropical rainforest
Desert
Temperate grassland

questions.explanation: Tropical rainforests have the highest net primary productivity among terrestrial biomes — abundant sunlight, warm year-round, consistently high rainfall. The Amazon, Congo and the Indonesian islands host most of Earth's rainforest. Tundra and deserts are among the least productive (cold / dry). Coral reefs and estuaries are the most productive aquatic biomes.

questions.stem: Lightning converts atmospheric nitrogen to nitrogen oxides, which wash down with rain and enrich the soil. This natural process contributes to the:

options.option_text: Phosphorus cycle
Nitrogen cycle
Carbon cycle
Sulphur cycle

questions.explanation: Lightning's intense energy breaks N₂-molecular bonds, letting N atoms combine with O to form NO and NO₂, which dissolve in rain as dilute nitric acid; soil bacteria convert these to usable nitrates. Estimated share of fixation — biological (~65 %), industrial Haber-Bosch (~25 %), lightning + volcanoes (~10 %). The phosphorus cycle, unusually, has no gaseous phase (moves via rocks, water, organisms).

questions.stem: The 'tenth percent rule' — stating that only a small fraction of energy is transferred between trophic levels — was proposed by:

options.option_text: Charles Elton
Raymond Lindeman
Arthur Tansley
Eugene Odum

questions.explanation: Raymond Lindeman (1942) proposed the 10 % law of energy transfer between trophic levels — basis for modern ecosystem ecology. Arthur Tansley coined the word 'ecosystem' (1935). Charles Elton pioneered the food-chain concept (1927). Eugene Odum wrote the influential textbook 'Fundamentals of Ecology' (1953) that helped standardise the field.

questions.stem: Unlike the carbon and nitrogen cycles, the phosphorus cycle lacks a significant gaseous phase. Which reservoir makes the phosphorus cycle fundamentally distinct from most other major biogeochemical cycles?

options.option_text: The atmosphere, where phosphorus exists as gaseous P₄ molecules
Rocks, minerals, and deep-ocean sediments on the seafloor
Living organisms, especially plant roots and mycorrhizal fungi
Freshwater bodies such as rivers, lakes, and tropical wetlands

questions.explanation: B is correct because phosphorus enters the cycle only through weathering of phosphate-bearing rocks (apatite) and upwelling of marine sediments — there is no atmospheric reservoir of phosphorus. Option A is wrong because phosphorus has no stable atmospheric gaseous form, unlike CO₂ or N₂. Option C is tempting because organisms do store phosphorus, but they are not the primary source — they depend entirely on rock weathering to obtain it.

questions.stem: An ecologist measures the total dry weight of all living organisms present in a pond ecosystem at a single point in time. Which ecological term most precisely describes this measurement?

options.option_text: Bioaccumulation — the buildup of toxins in an organism's tissues
Biomass — total mass of all living organisms in a given area
Biosphere — the zone of life extending from ocean floor to atmosphere
Biome — a major ecological community defined by climate and vegetation

questions.explanation: B is correct: biomass is expressed as dry mass per unit area (g/m²) and represents the total quantity of living matter at a given moment — precisely what an ecologist measures in the scenario. Option C (biosphere) refers to the global zone where life exists, not a measurable mass. Option D (biome) is a large-scale climate-vegetation community type such as tundra or tropical rainforest, not a mass measurement.

questions.stem: Excessive agricultural runoff carrying synthetic fertilizers triggers eutrophication in freshwater lakes, leading to algal blooms and oxygen depletion. Which pair of nutrients is the primary driver of this process?

options.option_text: Carbon dioxide and sulfur compounds leaching from the topsoil
Nitrogen compounds and phosphorus from synthetic fertilizer runoff
Calcium carbonate and magnesium salts carried in irrigation water
Iron oxides and potassium ions released from waterlogged paddy fields

questions.explanation: B is correct: nitrates and phosphates are the two nutrients that most strongly limit algal growth in freshwater. When artificially elevated by runoff, they cause explosive algal blooms. Oxygen depletion follows as bacteria decompose the dead algae. Option C (Ca/Mg) is wrong — while present in runoff, these minerals do not trigger algal blooms because algae are not limited by calcium or magnesium under typical conditions.

questions.stem: Sea otters in Pacific kelp forests prey on sea urchins; when otters were hunted to near-extinction, urchin populations exploded and reduced dense kelp beds to barren zones. Which ecological concept does this most precisely illustrate?

options.option_text: Apex predator — species occupying the highest trophic position always
Keystone species — one with disproportionately large ecosystem impact
Indicator species — reflects environmental health through population data
Pioneer species — the first coloniser of a newly disturbed habitat patch

questions.explanation: B is correct: a keystone species is defined not by its abundance or trophic rank but by the outsized effect its removal has on ecosystem structure. Sea otters are a textbook example — they are not the most numerous species yet their loss cascades through the entire food web. Option A is wrong because 'apex predator' simply describes trophic position; many apex predators are NOT keystone species, and vice versa.

questions.stem: In ecology, 'detritivores' play a specific and distinct role from both herbivores and true decomposers (bacteria/fungi). Which description correctly captures what detritivores do in biogeochemical cycling?

options.option_text: Synthesise organic matter via photosynthesis or chemosynthesis reactions
Physically fragment dead organic matter into smaller particles for decomposers
Chemically break down complex organics into inorganic mineral nutrients
Convert dissolved ammonia back to atmospheric N₂ through denitrification

questions.explanation: B is correct: detritivores (earthworms, millipedes, woodlice) physically shred and ingest detritus, massively increasing surface area for microbial decomposers to act upon — they do not chemically mineralise nutrients themselves. Option C describes the role of decomposers (bacteria and fungi), which is the most common confusion. Option D describes denitrifying bacteria, a completely different functional group in the nitrogen cycle.

questions.stem: In anaerobic zones of waterlogged soils and deep marine sediments, specialist bacteria use sulfate ions (SO₄²⁻) as a terminal electron acceptor instead of oxygen, releasing H₂S and producing the 'rotten-egg' odour. The technical name for this process is:

options.option_text: Assimilatory sulfate reduction — sulfate uptake for amino acid synthesis
Dissimilatory sulfate reduction by anaerobic sulfate-reducing bacteria
Sulfur oxidation by chemolithotrophic Thiobacillus in acidic mine drainage
Volatilisation of dimethyl sulfide released by marine phytoplankton cells

questions.explanation: B is correct: dissimilatory sulfate reduction (by genera such as Desulfovibrio and Desulfobacter) uses SO₄²⁻ purely as an electron acceptor for energy generation; the sulfur is not incorporated into biomass. Option A (assimilatory reduction) is the opposite — cells reduce a tiny amount of sulfate and build it into cysteine/methionine. Option C describes the reverse direction (oxidation of H₂S to SO₄²⁻). Option D (DMS volatilisation) is a real sulfur-cycle flux but involves algae releasing dimethylsulfoniopropionate, an entirely different pathway.

questions.stem: Alfred Redfield (1934) discovered that the C:N:P atomic ratio in marine phytoplankton (≈ 106:16:1) closely mirrors the dissolved inorganic nutrient ratios in deep ocean water. What is the most significant biogeochemical implication of this stoichiometric equivalence?

options.option_text: Ocean primary productivity is primarily limited by carbon dioxide availability
Marine biota and ocean chemistry are tightly co-regulated through nutrient cycling
Nitrogen is invariably the single limiting nutrient across all ocean ecosystems
Deep-ocean water composition is determined solely by riverine sediment inputs

questions.explanation: B is correct: the near-identical ratio in both organisms and deep water implies a feedback loop — marine life shapes ocean chemistry, and ocean chemistry constrains marine life, making the two tightly coupled. This has profound implications for modelling ocean productivity and climate. Option A is wrong because CO₂ is rarely limiting in the ocean; nitrogen and phosphorus are. Option C is wrong because the Redfield ratio itself (16:1 N:P) shows both N and P are important, and phosphorus limitation is common in freshwater systems while nitrogen limitation is more frequent in the open ocean.
